title: On Being and Unity (De Ente et Uno) — Angelology Passages

passages.incipit: Add the intellectual knowledge of divine minds, which the theologians call angels.
passages.quote_full: Add the intellectual knowledge of divine minds, which the theologians call angels. Even that is imperfect knowledge, at least because it seeks outside itself what it does not possess fully within itself, i.e., the light of truth which it lacks, and by which it is perfected.
passages.context: Pico argues that even angelic intellection is imperfect because angels seek truth outside themselves; only God possesses truth fully within himself. This establishes angels as created, participated beings dependent on divine illumination.
passages.metaphysical_concept: angel as participated intellect; angelic knowledge as imperfect participation in divine truth
passages.key_idea: Angels exemplify hierarchical being: their intellectual perfection depends on external divine illumination, marking them as creatures receiving being from God.
cross_references: Oration: angels as exemplars of intellect
Commento: angelic intellect as formal principle of human intellection
Heptaplus Layer 1: angels as intellect; Layer 2: angelic hierarchy as cosmic Nous
passages.scholiast_note: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II.2, q. 58 (On angelic knowledge as dependent on God's will and illumination)

passages.section: On imperfections in created beings continued
passages.incipit: But the life of the angels is not perfect.
passages.quote_full: But the life of the angels is not perfect. Unless the vivifying ray of divine light constantly warmed it, it would all fall into nothingness.
passages.context: Pico extends his analysis of imperfection to angelic life itself. Angels depend on continuous divine sustenance; without God's grace, they would return to non-being. This demonstrates the essential ontological hierarchy: God alone possesses independent being, all creatures derive being from God moment-by-moment.
passages.metaphysical_concept: angelic being as participated and dependent; divine light as sustaining principle of created existence
passages.key_idea: Angels embody the principle of participated being: their existence is not their own but continuously received from God's vivifying ray. This grounds the metaphysical hierarchy in which each level of being depends on the one above.
cross_references: Heptaplus Day 1, Layer 1: light as angelic intellect (divine illumination as creative principle)
Commento Book III: angelic ascent through divine love (eros as vivifying principle)
Oration: human ascent toward angelic nature via philosophical virtue
passages.scholiast_note: Plotinus, Enneads V.1 (On the eternal emanation of being from the One); Aquinas, Summa I, q. 104 (On conservation of creatures in being)

passages.section: On the four steps to God and divine darkness
passages.quote_full: Dionysius the Areopagite saw this. After all that he wrote in the Symbolic Theology, in the Theological Institutions, in On the Divine Names, and in On Mystical Theology, he finally at the end of that work spoke as he could about God in a very holy way, as if he were already in the cloud.
passages.context: Pico invokes Pseudo-Dionysius as exemplar of the mystical ascent toward God. Dionysius's hierarchical angelology is the framework for understanding how created beings (including angels) approach the divine darkness through successive negations and purifications.
passages.metaphysical_concept: Pseudo-Dionysius hierarchy as the path of negation and mystical ascent; angels as mediators in the negation of predicates
passages.key_idea: Pico locates Pseudo-Dionysius's angelology within a metaphysical framework: the nine angelic orders are themselves arranged in a hierarchy of being, each serving as a rung on the ladder of mystical ascent toward the unknowable divine darkness.
cross_references: Heptaplus Layer 2: Pseudo-Dionysius hierarchy explicitly mapped to creation narrative
Commento Book I: seraphim at apex of angelic hierarchy as exemplars of divine love
Oration: Pseudo-Dionysius's hierarchy invoked for dignity of human ascent
passages.source_location: Chapter Five (On the four steps), page 85, lines 2963-2966
passages.scholiast_note: Pseudo-Dionysius, De divinis nominibus, De mystica theologia (Works cited by Pico as authorities on angelic hierarchy and mystical theology)

passages.incipit: He is not truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom, nor one, nor unity, nor deity...
passages.quote_full: He is not truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom, nor one, nor unity, nor deity, nor goodness, nor spirit, so far as we can know him, nor does he have the name father or son nor any other of the things which are known to us or to anyone else in the world, nor is he any other of the things which are not nor any of the things which are, nor do the things which are know the divinity as it is, nor does it know the things which are as they are, nor is there any speaking of it, nor name nor science nor darkness nor light, nor error nor truth, neither is there any affirmation or negation of it.
passages.context: Pico quotes Pseudo-Dionysius's apophatic theology at length. The passage establishes God's radical transcendence beyond all being, one, and intelligibility. This is the apex of the hierarchy: even the highest angels (seraphim) cannot know God as God is; they approach only through negation.
passages.metaphysical_concept: apophatic theology; angelic intellection as necessarily limited by God's transcendent unknowability
passages.key_idea: The hierarchy of being culminates in God's radical transcendence. Angels, as the highest created intellects, cannot comprehend God; they can only know that He is not anything they can predicate. This establishes the ladder: matter → soul → human intellect → angelic intellect → divine darkness (unknowing).
cross_references: Heptaplus Layer 4: anagogical reading where angels lead mystical union
Commento Book III: seraphim's inability to fully comprehend divine essence despite perfect participation in divine love
Oration: human journey toward (but never fully achieving) angelic understanding
passages.source_location: Chapter Five (On mystical theology), page 85, lines 2968-2977 (quoting Pseudo-Dionysius, De mystica theologia V)
passages.scholiast_note: Howlett on Pico's Dionysian framework; Allen on negative theology and Plotinian emanation

passages.section: On being, one, true, good in created things
passages.incipit: All things that are after God have an efficient, exemplary, and final cause.
passages.quote_full: All things that are after God have an efficient, exemplary, and final cause. All things are from him, through him, and to him. If, therefore, we consider things as they are constituted by God as efficient cause, they are called beings, because they participate being from God as efficient cause.
passages.context: Pico establishes the framework for understanding created beings (including angels) as participants in being. All created things—angels, human souls, material bodies—receive their being from God as efficient cause and maintain their being through continuous participation.
passages.metaphysical_concept: participated being; creation as participation in divine being through efficient causality
passages.key_idea: The hierarchy of creation is grounded in degrees of participation. Angels, as pure intellects, participate in being most directly and continuously, requiring no matter or sense faculty.
cross_references: Heptaplus Layer 1-2: Creation narrative as emanation of being through hierarchical orders
Commento Book I-II: angelic hierarchy as exemplars of participated being
Oration: human dignity as participation in angelic and divine nature through intellection
passages.source_location: Chapter Eight (On being, one, true, good in created things), page 91, lines 3207-3211
passages.scholiast_note: Aquinas, Summa I, qq. 45-46 (On creation as participation); Plotinus, Enneads V.1 (On emanation)

passages.quote_full: One follows being. Truth is third, because after something is in itself, it must be seen whether it be like the exemplar according to which it was formed. If the thing is similar, it follows that it turns itself through goodness toward its exemplar as to the like and similar.
passages.context: Pico outlines the order of transcendental properties: being precedes one, one precedes truth, truth precedes goodness. This order applies to all created beings, including angels. The seraph, as the highest angel, exemplifies this order most perfectly: it has maximum being, unity, truth (conformity to its exemplar), and goodness (orientation toward God).
passages.metaphysical_concept: transcendental properties as hierarchical grades of perfection; seraph as exemplar of created unity
passages.key_idea: The transcendental hierarchy (being → one → true → good) is mirrored in the angelic hierarchy. Higher angels (seraphim, cherubim, thrones) possess greater unity, truth, and goodness; lower angels participate in these properties proportionally.
cross_references: Heptaplus Layer 2: angelic hierarchy as grades of unity and simplicity
Commento Book I: seraphim as 'unity' in the Sefirotic correspondence
Oration: human ascent through virtue toward angelic unity and goodness
passages.source_location: Chapter Eight (On properties in created things), page 92, lines 3223-3227
passages.scholiast_note: Aquinas, Summa I, q. 11 (On simplicity and transcendentals); Howlett on Pico's integration of transcendentals and hierarchy

passages.section: On evil and division as privation
passages.incipit: The false is the same as nothing. If we say that evil and nothing differ...
passages.quote_full: The reasons we have given above show that the false is the same as nothing. If we say that evil and nothing differ, the philosophers and theologians both will object, because to make evil is to make nothing, and it is customarily said that there is no efficient, but only a deficient cause of evil.
passages.context: Pico introduces the doctrine of evil as privation, not efficient causality. This is crucial for angelology: demons (fallen angels) are not positive forces of evil but privations of good. A demon is an angel deprived of charity, unity, and goodness—a hierarchical descent within angelic nature.
passages.metaphysical_concept: demonic as privation of angelic goodness; evil as ontological negation, not being
passages.key_idea: The metaphysical hierarchy includes a negative pole: just as seraphim represent the apex of participated being and unity, demons represent the descent into division and non-being. The fall is not the creation of a new substance but the privation of angelic goodness.
cross_references: Heptaplus Day 3, Layer 2: The fall and demonic obstruction as cosmic privation
Commento (implicit): Why love ascends to seraphim; why lust descends toward demonic
Oration: Human freedom to choose descent (toward bestiality and demonic) or ascent (toward angelhood)
passages.source_location: Chapter Eight (On opposites and evil), page 94, lines 3315-3326
passages.scholiast_note: Aquinas, Summa II.2, q. 64 (On the fall and demonic nature); Black on demonic privation in Heptaplus

passages.section: On division and loss of unity
passages.incipit: To divide a thing is the same as to destroy it.
passages.quote_full: To divide a thing is the same as to destroy it, and thus we cannot take away from anything its own natural unity in such a way that its being would nevertheless remain in its integrity. The whole is not its parts, but that one thing which emerges from the parts, as Aristotle teaches in First Philosophy, Book VIII.
passages.context: Pico establishes that division destroys unity and integrity. For angels, this means that any deviation from unified participation in divine being results in a loss of angelic nature and a descent toward non-being. The seraph's perfection lies in absolute unity with divine will; any division (as with fallen angels) is a privation of this unity.
passages.metaphysical_concept: unity as the ground of being and integrity; division as privation of unity
passages.key_idea: Angelic being is fundamentally unified. The seraph exemplifies perfect unity: no division between intellect and will, no multiplicity in understanding. A demon is an angel fractured by division from divine unity.
cross_references: Heptaplus Layer 2: Angelic separation of intelligible from material as hierarchical principle (not demonic division)
Commento Book I: Seraphim as perfect unity of love and intellect; lower angels as gradual divisions
Oration: Human soul's struggle to maintain unity against sensual division
passages.source_location: Chapter Eight (On whole and parts), page 94, lines 3328-3339
passages.scholiast_note: Aristotle, Metaphysics VII (On substance and unity); Plotinus, Enneads V.8 (On the One and emanation)

passages.section: On being, one, true, good in God and how they differ from created things
passages.incipit: They are not in God in relation to a cause that God does not have.
passages.quote_full: It follows from this knowledge that God is one, therefore no opposite can be conceived. See how those who imagine many principles, many gods, are in error. It follows immediately that God is most true. What does he who is existence itself have which might appear to be and not be? It follows certainly that he is truth itself.
passages.context: Pico contrasts God's mode of being, unity, and truth with created beings. While all creatures (including angels) have participated being, one, truth, and good (received from another), God possesses these identically and essentially. This establishes the absolute distinction between Creator and creation, which grounds the hierarchy: God is being itself; angels are beings by participation.
passages.metaphysical_concept: God's essential unity vs. creatures' participated unity; the Creator-creature distinction as ontological hierarchy
passages.key_idea: The hierarchy of being reaches its apex with God and descends through angels (pure intellects), human souls (rational-sensual hybrids), and matter. Each level has proportionally less unity, truth, and goodness because each participates rather than possesses these attributes essentially.
cross_references: Heptaplus Layer 2: Angelic hierarchy as reflection of divine simplicity in emanated form
Commento Book I: God as Chokmah (Wisdom, Unity) with seraphim as closest angels to divine unity
Oration: God as source of human dignity and capacity for ascent
passages.source_location: Chapter Nine (On being, one, true, good in God), page 95, lines 3353-3358
passages.scholiast_note: Aquinas, Summa I, q. 4 (On God's simplicity); Howlett on Pico's reconciliation of Aristotle and Plotinus regarding divine simplicity

passages.section: On God as cause and the reversal of transcendental order
passages.incipit: If we were to assign these four names to God as he is the cause of things...
passages.quote_full: If we were to assign these four names to God as he is the cause of things, the sequence must be reversed. First, he would be one, since he is understood in himself before he is understood as cause. Second, he would be good; third, true; fourth, being. Because the cause that is called the end is prior to the exemplary, and the exemplary cause prior to the efficient cause...
passages.context: Pico reveals that when God is understood as cause (not merely in Himself), the order of transcendentals reverses: one (unity of divine will) → good (final cause, God's perfect goodness drawing all things) → true (exemplary cause, God's ideas) → being (efficient cause, God creating and sustaining). This reversal illuminates angelic causality: each angel participates in this causal order, with higher angels (seraphim) receiving the final and exemplary causes more directly.
passages.metaphysical_concept: transcendental order as dependent on perspective (God in Himself vs. God as cause); angelic participation in divine causal orders
passages.key_idea: The angelic hierarchy mirrors the reversal of causal order: the highest angels are most directly moved by God's final cause (goodness) and exemplary cause (divine ideas); lower angels participate in these causes proportionally.
cross_references: Heptaplus Layer 6: Planetary angels as exemplars of final causes (why Jupiter is beneficent, Mars martial, etc.)
Commento Book I: Seraphim moved by divine love (final cause); lower angels by proportional good
Oration: Human ascent follows the causal order, from efficient (God makes us) through exemplary (we are images) to final (we seek God as highest good)
passages.source_location: Chapter Nine (On God as cause), page 95, lines 3379-3391
passages.scholiast_note: Aquinas, Summa I, q. 12 (On causal order); Howlett on Pico's integration of Pseudo-Dionysius (final/exemplary priority) and Aristotle (efficient causality)

passages.section: On living according to being, one, true, good
passages.incipit: Mind wanders here as a stranger, and approaches happiness insofar as it raises itself more and burns for divine things...
passages.quote_full: The present disputation seems above all to warn us that if we wish to be blessed, we must imitate the most blessed of all things, God, possessing in ourselves unity, truth, and goodness. Ambition disturbs the peace of unity and wrenches the soul that clings to it out of itself, and drags and tears the soul in pieces as if wounded.
passages.context: Pico concludes the metaphysical argument with an ethical exhortation: imitate God by possessing unity, truth, and goodness. The passage invokes the angelic paradigm: the seraph possesses perfect unity (undivided loyalty to God), perfect truth (total conformity to divine exemplar), and perfect goodness (complete charity and orientation toward God). Human souls, as rational beings, are called to approximate this angelic virtue.
passages.metaphysical_concept: angelology as ethical model; seraphic perfection as human aspiration
passages.key_idea: The metaphysical hierarchy becomes existential: humans, made in God's image and capable of angelic intellection, are summoned to imitate the angelic hierarchy in their own souls. The seraph exemplifies the unity, truth, and goodness that humans can aspire to through philosophy and virtue.
cross_references: Oration: Theme of human dignity through ascent to angelic nature and virtue
Commento Book III: Ascent through seraphic love as the fulfillment of the soul's journey
Heptaplus Layer 3 (Tropological): Angels as moral exemplars; humans called to their virtue
passages.source_location: Chapter Ten (On the ordering of life), page 96, lines 3413-3416
passages.scholiast_note: Ethics as applied metaphysics; Howlett on Pico's Dionysian-Thomistic fusion of being and virtue

passages.section: On unity, truth, goodness as the three cardinal virtues of the soul
passages.incipit: We are not one if we do not bind, by the union of virtue, sense bent downward with reason which looks at heavenly things.
passages.quote_full: We are not one if we do not bind, by the union of virtue, sense bent downward with reason which looks at heavenly things. If there are two princes in us, reigning in turns, as it were, we for a time follow God with the law of mind, for a time follow Baal with the law of the flesh, and our kingdom divided against itself is utterly desolated.
passages.context: Pico applies the metaphysics of unity to the human soul's internal hierarchy: reason (angelic) must rule over sense (bestial). Humans mirror the angelic-demonic conflict on a smaller scale. The seraph represents the ideal of unified reason and will; the demon represents fragmented disobedience.
passages.metaphysical_concept: human soul as microcosm of angelic hierarchy; virtue as harmonious subordination of lower to higher faculties
passages.key_idea: The angelic hierarchy models the human soul's proper order. Just as the seraphim preserve unified devotion to God, humans must unify their reason and sense through virtue, resisting the demonic fragmentation of will against reason.
cross_references: Oration: Human freedom to ascend (toward angelic order) or descend (toward bestial disorder or demonic fragmentation)
Commento Book III: The ascent of love that unifies the soul's faculties toward divine union
Heptaplus Layer 1-6: The integration of all worlds (elemental, celestial, angelic, human) as unified hierarchy
passages.source_location: Chapter Ten (On unity of virtue), page 96-97, lines 3433-3437
passages.scholiast_note: Aquinas, Summa II.1-2, (On virtue as harmonizing the soul's powers); Edelheit on Pico's psycho-spiritual integration

metadata.text: On Being and Unity (De Ente et Uno)
metadata.author: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
metadata.source_edition: Hackett Publishing Company, Inc., Indianapolis/Cambridge, 1998 (reprint); original Bobbs-Merrill, 1965
metaphysical_themes: Angel as participated intellect (vs. God's essential intellection)
Angelic being as dependent on divine sustenance and illumination
Seraph as exemplar of created unity approaching divine unity
Demon as privation of angelic goodness (not efficient evil cause)
Hierarchical structure of being: God (essential) → Angels (pure intellects) → Human souls (rational-sensual) → Matter
Transcendental properties (being, one, true, good) as grades of perfection mirrored in angelic hierarchy
Pseudo-Dionysius's angelology as framework for mystical ascent through degrees of being
Angelic intellection limited by God's transcendence (apophatic theology)
Angels as exemplars of human virtue (unity, truth, goodness)
Angelology as response to Platonist-Aristotelian debate: being and unity reconciled through hierarchical emanation

philosophical_lineages.pseudo-dionysius_celestial_hierarchy: Central: Nine angelic orders as cosmic Nous; apophatic theology; mystical ascent through degrees of being
philosophical_lineages.aquinas_scholastic_angelology: Angelic intellection as participated knowledge; conservation of creatures in being; transcendental properties; evil as privation
philosophical_lineages.plotinus_neoplatonic_emanation: Hierarchy of being flowing from the One; participated being at each level; souls' descent and ascent; intellectual intuition
philosophical_lineages.synthesis: Pico reconciles Aristotle's being with Plotinus's emanation via Pseudo-Dionysius's hierarchical angelology grounded in Aquinas's participation doctrine

scholarly_debate_notes.question: Is Pico's angelology truly Neoplatonic or fundamentally Scholastic?

positions.howlett: Synthesis: Pico reconciles Pseudo-Dionysius (Neoplatonic ladder) with Aquinas (participated being). The hierarchy is both Dionysian (orders of intellects) and Thomistic (degrees of participation).
positions.edelheit: Emphasis on Aquinas: Pico deepens Thomistic participation; angels exemplify how all creatures receive being from God moment-by-moment.
positions.allen: Emphasis on Plotinus: The entire structure is Plotinian emanation, with Pseudo-Dionysius providing the angelic ladder and Aquinas providing scholastic vocabulary.

scholarly_debate_notes.pico_position: All three are saying the same thing in different languages: Plotinus's hierarchy of being, Pseudo-Dionysius's hierarchies of intellects, and Aquinas's participation doctrine are one doctrine.

scholarly_debate_notes.question: How does Pico treat demons (fallen angels) metaphysically?

positions.black: Demons are privations of angelic goodness; the Fall disrupts the cosmic hierarchy but does not create a positive contrary principle.
positions.howlett: The demon's nature remains angelic (intellective, free), but will is turned from God—privation of orientation, not of substance.

scholarly_debate_notes.pico_position: Evil is privation of being and unity; demons exemplify how division from divine unity results in descent toward non-being.

gaps_and_observations: De Ente et Uno is less explicitly angelological than Heptaplus or Commento; angels are invoked as examples of participated being and hierarchical participation rather than as central subjects.
The work emphasizes angels' dependence on God and their position in the ontological hierarchy; it does not detail the nine orders or Pseudo-Dionysian distinctions (cf. Heptaplus Layer 2).
Sefirotic correspondences are absent (unlike Commento Book I); angelology here is purely metaphysical and theological, not magical or Kabbalistic.
No treatment of planetary angels or celestial names (cf. Heptaplus Layer 6).
The focus on human ascent toward angelic virtue (Chapter Ten) anticipates the Oration's theme of human dignity.

The apophatic theology (God's unknowability beyond all names) suggests that even the highest angels (seraphim) cannot know God as He is—a limit on angelic intellection not explicitly treated in Commento.
metadata.cross_text_synthesis: De Ente et Uno provides the metaphysical foundation for Pico's angelology across all texts: (1) Angels are participated beings, depending on divine illumination. (2) The seraph exemplifies the highest degree of created unity approaching divine unity. (3) Angelology grounds the hierarchy of being that justifies human dignity and ascent. (4) Demons represent the privation of angelic goodness, enabling Pico to avoid Cathar dualism. (5) The transcendental properties (being, one, true, good) are the measure of angelic perfection, making angelology an ethical as well as metaphysical doctrine.
